progressionAssessment.rationale: Introductory literary studies, classical rhetoric, Western philosophy and world archaeology are placed in the first year, before the 200-level work on Greek archaeology, stylistics, myth and epic, empires and ancient warfare, and before the third-year courses on ancient democratic heritage, persuasive communication, adaptation, interpretive theory, art-historical research and the archival research seminar. No scheduled course carries a formal prerequisite, every course is offered in its assigned term, and the one 100-level course placed in year two, Introduction to Western Art History, is a deliberate entry point into the Renaissance reception strand rather than a displaced foundation.

alternativeSelection.assessment: Two complete related-fields programmes are defensible. The first is the closest feasible response through classical literature in translation, rhetoric, ancient philosophy, archaeology, history and reception. The second uses the programme’s evidenced continuing influence of antiquity to build a substantively different political, legal and historical curriculum; twelve courses / 90 EC differ in each direction. A third programme centred on Greek and Latin language, philology, translation and original-text expertise is not feasible because the current UCR workbook contains no ancient-language sequence, Greek or Latin linguistics, or advanced original-text seminars. That central disciplinary gap remains explicit rather than being filled with general literature or communication courses.

Both study the reception and creative rewriting of inherited forms; UCR is a general creative-communication laboratory rather than a Greek-and-Latin reception course.
UCR reads Virgil in translation but has no Latin-language epic course.
UCR has no original-language course in late-antique and medieval Latin literature.

Both address the Hellenistic and Roman worlds and imperial development; UCR places Rome within a comparative study of empires.

Both interpret the ancient Near East and Greek world through cultural and material evidence; UCR embeds them in a global archaeological survey.
Both examine how places, objects and narratives become sites of memory; UCR focuses on ancient democracy and heritage rather than the comparator’s broader memory-studies course.
Both examine humanities knowledge and disciplinary interpretation; UCR does so through the historiography and practice of art history.

notes.text: The Greek and Latin Language and Culture programme combines cumulative Greek and Latin language acquisition, linguistics, translation and advanced reading of classical, late-antique and medieval texts in the original with literature, history, philosophy and material culture. UCR can approach classical antiquity through literature in translation, rhetoric, philosophy, archaeology, heritage, history, law and politics, but it does not teach Greek or Latin. The UCR programmes therefore offer related perspectives rather than a full Classics curriculum.

The external programme follows a fixed Greek-and-Latin disciplinary sequence, alongside 30 EC of approved profiling and a 12-EC thesis. UCR assembles related material across individually selected literature, communication, heritage, philosophy, history, law and politics courses; it has no separate ancient-language sequence, profiling block or scheduled thesis. Optional independent research is shown only as the standardized comparison element.
